title: The dog's legs
translation: Masafusa, a Major Counsellor, was a learned and good man, and the retired emperor was thinking of making him a general of the palace guards. Around that time, one of the emperor's attendants came to him and said, "I've just seen something horrible."
"Lord Masafusa cut the legs off a live dog to feed his hawk. I saw it through a hole in the fence."
The emperor was disgusted. From then on he was cold towards Masafusa, and the promotion never came.

It's surprising that a man like Masafusa kept hawks at all, but the story about the dog was made up. It's a pity for him that he was lied about. Still, the emperor heard about a thing like that and hated it, and that does him great credit.

Anyone who enjoys killing living things, or hurting them, or making them fight, is no better than the animals that tear each other apart. Look closely at any bird or beast, down to the smallest insect. They care for their young and miss their parents. They live in pairs. They get jealous and angry, they want things, they love themselves and cling to life. And because they have no wisdom at all, they feel all this even more strongly than we do. How can it not hurt to make them suffer, or to take their lives? If you can look at a living creature and feel no pity, you're not human.

literal: The Major Counsellor Masafusa was a person wise in learning and good, and at the time when (the retired emperor) thought he would like to make him a General, a person who was a close attendant of the retired emperor said, 'Just now I saw a shocking thing', and when (the retired emperor) asked, 'What is it?', he said, 'Lord Masafusa, to feed his hawk, cut off the legs of a live dog: I saw it through a hole in the fence between the grounds', and (the emperor) found him repellent and hateful, and his usual favour changed, and (Masafusa) was not promoted.
That such a person kept hawks is unexpected, but the dog's legs were a thing without basis.
The lie is a pity, but the heart of the lord who, hearing of such a thing, hated it, is a very admirable thing.
In general, people who kill living things, hurt them and make them fight, and play and enjoy it, are of the kind of beasts that harm and kill each other.

When one looks carefully at the state of all birds and beasts, even small insects, their caring for their children, being attached to their parents, keeping company as husband and wife, being jealous, being angry, having many desires, loving themselves and clinging to life is, because they are wholly ignorant, even greater than in humans.
To give them suffering and to take their lives: how could that not be painful?
Anyone who looks at all sentient beings and has no heart of compassion is not human.

notes.text: Minamoto no Masafusa (also called Tsuchimikado Masafusa), a court noble who became (provisional) Major Counsellor ({大納言|だいなごん}) in 1295 and died in 1302, aged 41. {才|ざえ}: learning, as in section 1.

{大将|だいしやう}: a General of the Palace Guards, one of the highest posts at court, for which only nobles of the top families were chosen. ばや: 'I would like to'. The one who wants to promote him is the {院|ゐん}, the retired emperor, Several retired emperors were alive at the time, and commentators do not agree which one is meant; Kameyama (1249–1305) is one suggestion.
{飼|か}ふ here means 'to feed'. Hawks for falconry were fed on meat. Falconry was a sport of warriors and of some nobles, and Buddhist teaching frowned on it because it lives on killing.

notes.quote: 犬の足はあとなき事なり
notes.text: あとなし: 'without a trace', so 'groundless, made up'. Kenkō states it as a fact: the hawk was real, the dog was not.
{不便|ふびん}: 'pitiful, unfortunate', written today as {不憫|ふびん}. A false friend: modern {不便|ふべん} means 'inconvenient'. It is a pity for Masafusa, whose career the lie ended.

{畜生|ちくしやう}: animals, the realm of beasts, one of the six paths of rebirth in Buddhism. People who torment animals for fun belong with beasts that kill each other. Modern ちくしょう, 'damn it', comes from the same word.

{愚痴|ぐち}: a Buddhist term, 'ignorance, delusion', the lack of the insight that would free a being from its attachments. Animals have none, so their attachments are even stronger. Modern {愚痴|ぐち} means 'complaining', a false friend.
{有情|うじやう}: Buddhist term for all beings with feelings, animals as well as people, as opposed to {非情|ひじやう}, things without feeling such as plants and stones.
{人倫|じんりん}: 'a human being, humanity'. The section moves from court gossip to a Buddhist argument and ends on this flat verdict.
